newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerian opposition and papers blast Arabic drive.
newsitem.headline: Algerian opposition and papers blast Arabic drive.

text.p: Algerian newspapers and a secular opposition party on Wednesday attacked the country's government for passing a law making Arabic compulsory in public life, saying this would worsen Algeria's crisis.
But a senior official said the North African country must bolster its identity through promoting Arabic or Algeria would become an unkown quantity among other nations.

The French-language daily Le Matin, summing up influential French-speaking elite in Algeria's higher economic and cultural echelons, said it agreed with those who dubbed the law a "form of terrorism" and a "willingness to divide the country".
"It is a new form of provocation which spawns fiercely another fracture in Algerian society," said the secular opposition Rally for Democracy and Culture (RCD) party.
RCD leader Said Saadi won about 10 percent of the vote in last year's presidential poll.
The government-appointed quasi-parliament, the Transitional National Council (CNT), on Tuesday passed the new law banning officials from making public statements in any language but Arabic.
Under the law, officials who write or sign memos or correspondences in foreign languages can be fined up to 5,000 dinars ($91) or up to 10,000 dinars ($182) if they reoffend.
The measure, which results in curbing French used more easily by many government ministers and officials, was called on Wednesday a "demagogic" move by the French-language El Watan.

"What sort of mankind endowed with reason can imagine for one instant that public life may be totally Arabised by July 1998 and university courses completely ensured in Arabic within the next four years," asked El Watan, one of Algeria's most influential daily newspapers.
The law states that the "process of generalising the use of the Arabic language should be perfected by July 5, 1998" and teaching in universities in Arabic must be in place in 2000.

Liberte newspaper, giving as example that government ministers suffered the experience of trying to make statements in Arabic, said "Arabising a country during a two-year-period while it is going through a deep crisis will not be an easy task".

A spokesman from the main secular Socialist Forces Front (FFS) party, which led a massive street march early in 1990 to protest previous government moves to bring in Arabisation, said on Wednesday the party leadership needed time to look carefully into the new law before deciding on its reaction.
Abdelkader Bensalah, CNT speaker, in a statement reasserting Algerian leaders' constant drive to wean the country from the culture of former colonial power, France, said:
"Everyone knows that knowledge and culture have no nationality. It is a fact. But a nation without distinguished language is a nation which has no role or real influence."
